topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.222, when a partnership, association, or corporation applies for a broker's license, which individuals -- beyond the designated broker of record -- must independently hold a current PA salesperson or broker license?
choice_a: Each member of the partnership/association, or each officer of the corporation, who intends to engage in the real estate business
choice_b: No one else -- only the broker of record needs any license at all
choice_c: Every shareholder or partner, regardless of whether they engage in real estate activity
choice_d: Only the entity's bookkeeper or accountant
explanation: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.222 requires that each member of the partnership or association, or each officer of the corporation, who intends to engage in the real estate business hold either a current standard or reciprocal license as a salesperson or broker -- a requirement that runs alongside, and is narrower than, RELRA Section 513's broker-of-record qualification rule.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.222 (confirmed, quoted via Cornell LII regulation excerpt)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Does a corporate shareholder or limited partner who does NOT personally engage in the real estate business need to hold a real estate license under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.222?
choice_a: No -- the individual-licensing requirement for members/officers of a licensed entity applies only to those who intend to engage in the real estate business, not to passive investors
choice_b: Yes -- every shareholder or limited partner must be licensed regardless of their role
choice_c: Yes, but only if they own more than 50% of the entity
choice_d: No individual within a licensed entity is ever required to hold a license
explanation: Section 35.222's licensing requirement is expressly tied to intent to engage in the real estate business -- a passive shareholder or limited partner with no active brokerage role falls outside that requirement, even though the entity itself and its broker of record must still be properly licensed.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.222 (confirmed)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: When a corporation applies for a Pennsylvania broker's license, is the license issued to the corporation itself, or only to the individual broker of record?
choice_a: The corporation, as the business entity, is the actual licensee, separate and apart from the individual license the broker of record must also hold in his or her own right
choice_b: Only the broker of record is licensed; the corporation itself never holds any license
choice_c: The license attaches to the corporation's registered agent, not the corporation or the broker of record
choice_d: Corporations cannot hold real estate broker licenses under any circumstance in Pennsylvania
explanation: RELRA contemplates the corporation, partnership, or association as the actual license applicant/holder, while Section 513 separately requires the individual designated as broker of record to independently satisfy Sections 511 and 512 -- meaning both the entity and the individual broker of record carry distinct licensing statuses.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.513 (confirmed verbatim); entity-vs-individual licensure structure is standard business-licensing doctrine, hedge: general reasoning from the statute's text rather than an independently pinpoint-cited interpretive source

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Within how many days following the death of a broker of record must a partner or corporate officer file an application with the Commission designating a new broker of record?
choice_a: 15 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 60 days
choice_d: 90 days
explanation: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.253 requires that, within 15 days following the death of a broker of record, a partner or corporate officer of the licensed entity file an application with the Commission designating another individual to serve as broker of record -- allowing the business to continue operating under new leadership.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.253 (confirmed, quoted via Cornell LII regulation excerpt)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: If a corporation's or partnership's broker of record becomes unable to act due to illness or injury (rather than death), what must the entity do under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.254?
choice_a: Notify the Commission within 15 days that it has appointed another licensed broker to act as INTERIM broker of record until the original broker of record can resume duties
choice_b: Immediately and permanently dissolve the entity's broker license
choice_c: Do nothing until the broker of record either recovers or dies
choice_d: Wait 90 days before any notification is required
explanation: Section 35.254 requires the corporate officer, partner, or the sole-proprietor broker's attorney-in-fact to notify the Commission within 15 days of appointing an interim broker or broker of record when illness or injury prevents the original broker from acting -- a temporary substitution, distinct from the permanent replacement required after a death under Section 35.253.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.254 (confirmed, adopted December 10, 2004, effective December 11, 2004, 34 Pa.B. 6530)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: When a broker operating as a SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP (not a corporation or partnership) dies, what must the estate do under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.252, and how does this differ from an entity's options after its broker of record dies?
choice_a: The estate must, within 15 days, notify the Commission that it has appointed a licensed broker to supervise the TERMINATION of the deceased broker's business -- unlike a corporation or partnership, a sole proprietorship cannot simply appoint a new broker of record and continue operating indefinitely
choice_b: The sole proprietorship automatically converts into a corporation upon the broker's death
choice_c: Nothing -- sole proprietorships terminate automatically with no estate notification required
choice_d: The estate has 5 years to find a replacement broker before any business licenses lapse
explanation: Section 35.252 requires the deceased sole-proprietor broker's estate to notify the Commission within 15 days that it has appointed a licensed broker to supervise winding down the business -- a fundamentally different outcome than Section 35.253's entity-continuation process, since a sole proprietorship's license is tied to the individual rather than a separately licensed business entity.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.252 (confirmed, contrasted with Section 35.253)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: During the termination period following a sole-proprietor broker's death, what is the appointed supervising broker expressly PROHIBITED from doing under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.252?
choice_a: Entering into new listing agreements on behalf of the deceased broker's business
choice_b: Allowing pending agreements of sale or lease to proceed to consummation
choice_c: Promoting unexpired existing listing agreements
choice_d: Communicating with the deceased broker's former clients at all
explanation: Section 35.252 permits the supervising broker to promote unexpired listings (unless the seller/lessor cancels) and to let pending sale/lease agreements proceed to closing, but expressly bars entering into any NEW listing agreements during the wind-down period -- the business is being closed out, not expanded.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.252 (confirmed)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.252, unexpired listing agreements of a deceased sole-proprietor broker automatically expire how many days after the broker's death if not otherwise cancelled?
choice_a: 90 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 180 days
choice_d: 15 days
explanation: Section 35.252 provides that unexpired listing agreements may be promoted during the termination period but automatically expire 90 days after the broker's death and may not be renewed -- a hard outer limit on how long a sole proprietorship's business can be wound down under a supervising broker.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.252 (confirmed)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: RELRA Section 513 names three types of business applicants that can hold a broker's license through a broker of record. Which of the following is NOT one of the three entity types the statute's text actually enumerates?
choice_a: Limited liability company
choice_b: Corporation
choice_c: Partnership
choice_d: Association
explanation: Section 513's actual text refers only to 'a corporation, partnership or association' -- reflecting RELRA's original drafting era. Modern brokerages commonly organize as LLCs, but Section 513 itself does not use that specific term; practitioners generally treat an LLC as falling within the broader 'association' concept for licensing purposes.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.513 (confirmed verbatim -- statute names only corporation, partnership, association); LLC treatment as an 'association' is standard practitioner understanding, hedge: not independently pinpoint-cited to a Commission interpretive ruling in this pass

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under RELRA Section 513, must the individual designated as broker of record for a licensed entity satisfy ONLY the broker qualification standards of Section 511, or must that individual also comply with the application procedures of Section 512?
choice_a: Both -- Section 513 requires the broker of record to satisfy the provisions of Section 511 (qualifications) AND Section 512 (application) as if applying individually
choice_b: Only Section 511's qualifications; Section 512's application procedures do not apply to a broker of record
choice_c: Only Section 512's application procedures; qualification standards are waived for entity brokers of record
choice_d: Neither -- the entity's own application substitutes entirely for the broker of record's compliance with 511 or 512
explanation: Section 513's text applies 'the provisions of sections 511 and 512' jointly to the individual designated as broker of record -- meaning that person must meet both the substantive qualification standards of Section 511 and go through the application process of Section 512, just as an individual broker applicant would.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.513 (confirmed verbatim)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: In general business law, what is the defining liability characteristic of a SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP?
choice_a: The owner has unlimited personal liability for all business debts and obligations, since the law does not recognize the business as legally separate from the owner
choice_b: The owner's liability is automatically capped at the amount invested in the business
choice_c: Sole proprietorships are legally required to carry a minimum of $1 million in liability insurance
choice_d: The owner has no liability at all for business debts under any circumstance
explanation: A sole proprietorship is the simplest business form precisely because it creates no legal separation between the owner and the business -- the owner bears unlimited personal liability for business debts and any judgments against the business, a foundational general-business-law concept relevant to a broker deciding how to structure a brokerage.
source_note: hedge: standard general business law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: In a GENERAL partnership, how is liability for the partnership's debts and obligations generally allocated among the partners?
choice_a: Each general partner is personally, jointly and severally liable for the partnership's debts, and each partner can generally bind the partnership through the doctrine of mutual agency
choice_b: No partner has any personal liability; only the partnership entity itself can ever be sued
choice_c: Liability is automatically capped at each partner's percentage ownership interest, similar to a corporation
choice_d: Only the managing partner bears any personal liability; other partners are fully shielded
explanation: In a general partnership, each partner is personally, jointly and severally liable for partnership debts, and under the mutual-agency doctrine each general partner can bind the partnership in dealings with third parties -- a meaningfully different (and riskier) liability profile than a corporation or LLC.
source_note: hedge: standard general business/partnership law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What structural feature must every LIMITED partnership have, distinguishing it from a general partnership?
choice_a: At least one general partner who retains unlimited personal liability and management authority, alongside one or more limited partners whose liability is capped at their investment
choice_b: All partners automatically have limited liability, with no general partner required
choice_c: A limited partnership may never have more than two total partners
choice_d: Limited partners must personally manage the day-to-day business to retain their limited-liability status
explanation: A limited partnership requires at least one general partner who retains unlimited liability and management control, while limited partners' liability is capped at their capital contribution -- but limited partners generally must avoid taking an active management role, or they risk being treated as general partners for liability purposes.
source_note: hedge: standard general business/partnership law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What is the defining liability and existence characteristic of a CORPORATION as a business entity?
choice_a: A corporation is a separate legal 'person' distinct from its shareholders, whose liability is generally limited to their investment, and the corporation has perpetual existence independent of any single owner's death or departure
choice_b: A corporation's shareholders are always personally liable for corporate debts, just like general partners
choice_c: A corporation automatically dissolves whenever any single shareholder dies or sells their shares
choice_d: A corporation cannot own real property in its own name under general business law
explanation: A corporation is a distinct legal entity that can sue, be sued, own property, and enter contracts in its own name; shareholders' liability is generally limited to their investment, and the corporation's existence continues independent of any individual shareholder's death, departure, or share transfer -- unlike a sole proprietorship or general partnership.
source_note: hedge: standard general business/corporate law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What is the key tax distinction between a standard C-corporation and an S-corporation or LLC electing pass-through taxation?
choice_a: A C-corporation is subject to 'double taxation' -- the corporation pays tax on its profits, and shareholders pay tax again on dividends -- while an S-corporation or pass-through LLC's income is taxed only once, at the individual owner level
choice_b: An S-corporation pays corporate-level tax twice, while a C-corporation is never taxed at all
choice_c: LLCs are always taxed as C-corporations by default, with no other option available
choice_d: There is no meaningful tax distinction between these entity types under federal law
explanation: A C-corporation's profits are taxed at the corporate level, and then again at the shareholder level when distributed as dividends ('double taxation'); an S-corporation or an LLC that elects pass-through tax treatment avoids that second layer, with income instead flowing directly to owners' individual tax returns -- a standard consideration when brokers choose how to organize a brokerage.
source_note: hedge: standard federal general business/tax law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What business-structure advantage does a limited liability company (LLC) generally offer, compared to a general partnership or sole proprietorship?
choice_a: Members' personal liability for the LLC's debts is generally limited to their investment, similar to a corporation, while the LLC can still often retain the flexible pass-through tax treatment of a partnership
choice_b: LLC members are automatically subject to double taxation, just like C-corporation shareholders
choice_c: An LLC cannot have more than one member under general business law
choice_d: LLCs are legally identical to general partnerships in every respect, including liability exposure
explanation: The LLC is a hybrid entity: it generally shields members from personal liability for the entity's debts (like a corporation) while typically retaining the flexible pass-through tax treatment associated with partnerships -- a combination that has made it a popular structure for real estate brokerages and investment entities alike.
source_note: hedge: standard general business/LLC law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: What document must be filed with the Pennsylvania Department of State to form a Pennsylvania limited liability company?
choice_a: A Certificate of Organization, under 15 Pa.C.S. Section 8821
choice_b: Articles of Incorporation, identical to those used to form a corporation
choice_c: A Partnership Registration Statement
choice_d: No filing is required; an LLC exists automatically once members agree orally to form one
explanation: Under 15 Pa.C.S. Section 8821, a Pennsylvania LLC is formed by filing a Certificate of Organization (accompanied by a docketing statement) with the Department of State's Bureau of Corporations and Charitable Organizations -- distinct from the Articles of Incorporation used to form a corporation.
source_note: 15 Pa.C.S. Section 8821 (confirmed via Justia primary-source excerpt of the Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: In general business law, what is a Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT), and what is one key requirement it must satisfy to maintain its favorable pass-through tax treatment?
choice_a: A specialized entity that pools investor capital to own and/or finance income-producing real estate, and which must distribute substantially all of its taxable income to shareholders annually to maintain its tax status
choice_b: A type of individual real estate license reserved exclusively for commercial appraisers
choice_c: A government agency that regulates real estate brokerages
choice_d: A REIT is functionally identical to a sole proprietorship and offers no liability protection
explanation: A REIT is a business entity, often structured as a trust or corporation, that pools capital to invest in income-producing real estate; to qualify for favorable pass-through tax treatment, a REIT must distribute substantially all (generally at least 90%) of its taxable income to shareholders each year, among other structural requirements.
source_note: hedge: standard national general business law doctrine regarding REITs, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: How does a joint venture, as a business structure, generally differ from an ordinary ongoing partnership?
choice_a: A joint venture is formed by two or more parties to combine resources for a specific, limited-purpose project (such as one development), and typically dissolves once that project is completed, unlike an ongoing partnership formed for a continuing business
choice_b: A joint venture is legally identical to a corporation in every respect
choice_c: A joint venture can never involve more than one licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Joint ventures automatically last in perpetuity, unlike partnerships
explanation: A joint venture is a business-law concept describing two or more parties (individuals or entities) combining resources and expertise for a specific, limited-purpose undertaking -- commonly a single real estate development -- and it generally terminates once that project concludes, unlike a general partnership formed for an ongoing business.
source_note: hedge: standard general business law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under the general business-law doctrine of 'piercing the corporate veil,' when might a court hold a corporation's or LLC's owners personally liable for the entity's debts despite the entity's normal liability shield?
choice_a: When the owners fail to maintain corporate formalities, commingle personal and business funds, or use the entity as a mere shell to perpetrate fraud or injustice
choice_b: Automatically, any time the entity fails to turn a profit in its first year
choice_c: Only when the entity's annual revenue exceeds $1 million
choice_d: Never -- the liability shield of a corporation or LLC cannot be overcome under any circumstance
explanation: 'Piercing the corporate veil' is the equitable doctrine under which courts disregard an entity's normal liability shield and hold owners personally responsible -- typically when formalities are ignored, funds are commingled, or the entity is used as an alter ego to commit fraud or avoid an existing obligation.
source_note: hedge: standard general business/corporate law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under Pennsylvania's Fictitious Names Act, 54 Pa.C.S. Section 311, what must a brokerage entity do if it plans to conduct business under a name other than its own true legal name?
choice_a: Register the fictitious/assumed name with the Pennsylvania Department of State's Corporation Bureau
choice_b: Nothing -- fictitious business names require no state-level registration in Pennsylvania
choice_c: Register the name only with the local county recorder of deeds, never with the state
choice_d: Obtain a separate broker's license for the fictitious name, distinct from the entity's actual license
explanation: The Fictitious Names Act requires any individual, sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC, or other association conducting business under an assumed name to register that name with the Department of State via an Application for Registration of Fictitious Name -- a general business-law filing requirement separate from (though it interacts with) RELRA's own business-name-on-license rule.
source_note: 54 Pa.C.S. Section 311 (confirmed via Department of State and FindLaw primary-source excerpts)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under general common-law agency principles applicable to real estate practice, which mnemonic is commonly used to describe the fiduciary duties an agent owes to a principal?
choice_a: Care, Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Accounting, and Confidentiality
choice_b: Speed, Efficiency, Volume, and Aggressiveness
choice_c: Only Loyalty -- the other traditional fiduciary duties do not apply to real estate agents
choice_d: Profit, Growth, Market Share, and Client Retention
explanation: The classic common-law fiduciary-duty mnemonic -- Care, Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Accounting, and Confidentiality -- describes the general duties an agent owes a principal, forming the doctrinal backdrop against which RELRA's own statutory agency-duty provisions (covered separately in this bank's Agency Law bucket) were written.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate agency-law doctrine, not Pennsylvania-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Is a licensee's ethical obligation under a voluntary professional code of ethics (such as the NAR Code of Ethics) the same thing as their legal obligation under RELRA?
choice_a: No -- ethics codes are professional standards that can be more demanding than the law in some respects, and violating a voluntary ethics code does not automatically constitute a RELRA violation, or vice versa
choice_b: Yes -- ethics codes and RELRA are legally identical documents enforced by the same body in the same way
choice_c: No -- ethics codes have no relationship whatsoever to real estate practice
choice_d: Yes -- a licensee who violates the NAR Code of Ethics automatically has their PA license revoked
explanation: Professional ethics codes are distinct from licensing law: they are typically enforced by professional associations (not the State Real Estate Commission) and often set standards that go beyond RELRA's minimum legal requirements, so conduct can violate one without automatically violating the other, even though the two frequently overlap in substance.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate ethics-vs-law distinction, not Pennsylvania-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Does the NAR (National Association of REALTORS) Code of Ethics legally bind every real estate licensee in Pennsylvania?
choice_a: No -- the NAR Code of Ethics binds only licensees who are also members of the REALTOR association (REALTORS); non-member licensees are not subject to it, though all licensees remain subject to RELRA regardless of association membership
choice_b: Yes -- every PA real estate licensee is automatically a REALTOR and bound by the Code of Ethics
choice_c: No -- the NAR Code of Ethics has been fully incorporated into RELRA and applies identically to every licensee
choice_d: The NAR Code of Ethics applies only to brokers, never to salespersons, regardless of membership
explanation: 'REALTOR' is a trademarked designation for members of the National Association of REALTORS and its affiliated boards; only those member licensees are contractually bound by (and disciplined under) the NAR Code of Ethics, while every PA licensee -- member or not -- remains independently subject to RELRA and Commission regulations.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate industry doctrine regarding NAR/REALTOR membership, not Pennsylvania-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Does a licensee's general duty of honesty and fair dealing extend to a customer/third party the licensee does NOT represent, or only to the licensee's own client/principal?
choice_a: A licensee owes basic honesty and fair dealing to all parties in a transaction, even non-clients, while the deeper fiduciary duties (loyalty, obedience, full disclosure, confidentiality) are owed only to the licensee's own client/principal
choice_b: A licensee owes literally no duty of any kind to anyone who is not their own client
choice_c: A licensee owes full fiduciary-level duties equally to every person involved in a transaction, with no distinction between clients and customers
choice_d: Duties of honesty apply only to commercial transactions, never to residential ones
explanation: General real estate practice doctrine distinguishes 'customers' (to whom a licensee owes basic fairness, honesty, and disclosure of material facts) from 'clients' (to whom the licensee owes the full, deeper set of fiduciary duties) -- a distinction that underlies Pennsylvania's own designated-agency and transaction-licensee framework covered elsewhere in this bank.
source_note: hedge: standard national agency-law distinction between customer-level fair dealing and client-level fiduciary duty, not Pennsylvania-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: As a general ethical and fiduciary principle (distinct from any single RELRA provision), why must a licensee disclose any personal or financial interest they hold in a transaction to their principal?
choice_a: Because an undisclosed personal interest creates a conflict between the licensee's own financial incentives and their fiduciary duty of loyalty to the principal, undermining the trust the agency relationship depends on
choice_b: Because disclosure is purely a courtesy with no legal or ethical significance
choice_c: Because only licensed attorneys, not real estate licensees, are ever subject to conflict-of-interest concerns
choice_d: Because conflicts of interest are impossible to create in a principal-agent relationship
explanation: The general ethical rationale for conflict-of-interest disclosure is that a fiduciary's own financial or personal stake in a deal can compromise their duty of undivided loyalty to the principal -- the foundational reasoning behind more specific statutory rules (such as RELRA's own self-dealing disclosure requirements, covered elsewhere in this bank) rather than an isolated technicality.
source_note: hedge: standard national fiduciary-ethics doctrine underlying conflict-of-interest disclosure rules, not tied to one specific RELRA citation in this question

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: If two competing brokerages in the same market agree between themselves to refuse to show listings from, or cooperate with, a discount brokerage that undercuts standard commission rates, what antitrust concept does this describe?
choice_a: A group boycott -- an agreement among competitors to collectively exclude or refuse to deal with another market participant, generally illegal under federal antitrust law
choice_b: A lawful exercise of each brokerage's independent business judgment, since no formal written contract was signed
choice_c: Market allocation, not a group boycott, because it involves refusing a specific competitor
choice_d: A legitimate MLS rule that antitrust law does not reach
explanation: A 'group boycott' occurs when two or more competitors agree to collectively refuse to deal with (or exclude) another market participant -- such as coordinating to freeze out a discount brokerage -- and is treated as a serious, often per se, violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act, regardless of whether the agreement is written or merely understood.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust doctrine as applied to real estate brokerage (Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1); Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, Section IV.D.4 (confirmed general subject matter)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: If two competing brokerages agree to divide a metropolitan area geographically -- each promising not to actively solicit listings or buyers in the other's assigned territory -- what antitrust violation does this describe?
choice_a: Market allocation -- an illegal agreement among competitors to divide up territories, customer types, or price ranges to avoid competing with each other
choice_b: A legitimate and common MLS territorial designation with no antitrust implications
choice_c: Price fixing, since territory and price are legally identical concepts under antitrust law
choice_d: This is only illegal if the brokerages are affiliated with the same franchise
explanation: 'Market allocation' describes competitors agreeing to divide up geographic territories, customer segments, or price tiers so they no longer directly compete with one another -- a per se violation of federal antitrust law that is analytically distinct from, though related to, price-fixing and group boycotts.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust doctrine as applied to real estate brokerage (Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1); Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, Section IV.D.4 (confirmed general subject matter)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: A broker who owns vacant land refuses to sell it to an interested builder unless the builder also agrees to list the builder's own separate properties exclusively with the broker's firm. What antitrust concept does this scenario describe?
choice_a: A tying (or tie-in) arrangement -- conditioning the sale of one product or service on the buyer also purchasing a separate, unrelated product or service
choice_b: A group boycott, since it involves only two parties rather than a group
choice_c: This is a routine and fully legal business negotiation with no antitrust dimension
choice_d: Market allocation, because it involves a geographic exchange of property
explanation: A 'tying arrangement' occurs when a party conditions the sale of one product or service (here, the vacant land) on the buyer also purchasing a separate, unrelated product or service (an exclusive listing agreement) -- a practice that can violate antitrust law when it improperly leverages market power in one market to force business in another.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust doctrine as applied to real estate brokerage; Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, Section IV.D.4 (confirmed general subject matter)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Which section of the federal Sherman Antitrust Act specifically addresses agreements among competitors (such as price-fixing, group boycotts, or market allocation), as opposed to a single firm's unlawful monopolization?
choice_a: Section 1, which prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies in restraint of trade
choice_b: Section 2, which exclusively governs agreements among two or more competitors
choice_c: The Sherman Act contains no distinct sections; all antitrust violations are treated identically
choice_d: Section 7, which deals only with corporate mergers
explanation: Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that unreasonably restrain trade -- the provision under which concerted brokerage conduct like price-fixing, group boycotts, and market allocation is analyzed -- while Section 2 separately addresses unilateral monopolization or attempted monopolization by a single dominant firm.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust doctrine (Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. Sections 1-2), not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Is it a violation of federal antitrust law for a single, independent brokerage to unilaterally decide, on its own, what commission rate it will charge clients?
choice_a: No -- a single firm's independent, unilateral decision about its own pricing is not an antitrust violation; the Sherman Act targets agreements between competitors, not one firm's own business judgment
choice_b: Yes -- any commission rate a broker sets is automatically illegal price-fixing
choice_c: Only illegal if the rate is below the local average
choice_d: Only illegal if the rate is above the local average
explanation: Antitrust law targets concerted action -- agreements between two or more competitors -- not the independent pricing decisions of a single firm; a brokerage remains free to unilaterally set, and even publicly advertise, its own commission structure without violating the Sherman Act, so long as it isn't coordinating that decision with competitors.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust doctrine distinguishing unilateral conduct from concerted action under Sherman Act Section 1, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Can informal, casual conversations about commission rates or splits among competing brokers at an MLS meeting or local real estate association gathering create antitrust exposure, even without a formal written agreement?
choice_a: Yes -- an illegal price-fixing or market-allocation agreement can be inferred from informal conduct and conversation alone; no signed contract is required for an antitrust violation to exist
choice_b: No -- antitrust law requires a signed, written contract before any violation can occur
choice_c: No -- MLS meetings and association gatherings are entirely exempt from antitrust scrutiny
choice_d: Only if the conversation is recorded on video
explanation: Antitrust violations can be established through circumstantial evidence of a 'meeting of the minds' -- informal conversations, understandings, or a consistent pattern of parallel conduct following such discussions can support an inference of an illegal agreement, which is precisely why brokers are commonly advised never to discuss commission rates or splits with competitors, even casually.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust-compliance guidance for real estate practice, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Which two federal agencies are principally responsible for enforcing antitrust law against anticompetitive practices in the real estate brokerage industry?
choice_a: The U.S. Department of Justice's Antitrust Division and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
choice_b: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
choice_c: The Pennsylvania State Real Estate Commission and the PA Attorney General exclusively
choice_d: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
explanation: Federal antitrust enforcement in the real estate industry, as in other industries, is principally carried out by the U.S. Department of Justice's Antitrust Division and the Federal Trade Commission -- separate from, and in addition to, the Pennsylvania State Real Estate Commission's own licensing-discipline authority under RELRA.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust-enforcement doctrine, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Beyond civil liability, what kind of exposure can an individual face for a serious antitrust violation such as participating in a price-fixing conspiracy?
choice_a: Criminal exposure, including substantial fines and potential imprisonment, in addition to civil damages and license discipline
choice_b: No consequences beyond a strongly worded warning letter
choice_c: Antitrust violations can only ever result in civil, never criminal, liability
choice_d: Automatic dissolution of the individual's marriage under federal law
explanation: Serious antitrust violations, particularly per se offenses like price-fixing, can carry criminal penalties -- including significant fines and imprisonment for individuals -- on top of civil treble-damages exposure and any separate professional license discipline, underscoring why antitrust compliance training is a standard part of brokerage risk management.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust doctrine regarding criminal exposure under the Sherman Antitrust Act, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Is it automatically an illegal 'group boycott' for one individual brokerage to independently decide, for its own legitimate business reasons, not to cooperate with a particular competing brokerage?
choice_a: No -- a single firm's independent, unilateral refusal to deal with a specific competitor is not automatically illegal; a group boycott requires concerted action among two or more competitors agreeing together to exclude someone
choice_b: Yes -- any refusal to cooperate with a competitor is automatically an illegal group boycott regardless of how many firms are involved
choice_c: No -- group boycotts can never be illegal under any circumstances
choice_d: Yes, but only if the refusing brokerage has fewer than 5 employees
explanation: The antitrust concern with 'group boycotts' is specifically the CONCERTED aspect -- two or more competitors coordinating to jointly exclude a market participant; a single brokerage's own independent, unilateral decision not to cooperate with a particular competitor for legitimate business reasons does not, by itself, constitute an illegal boycott.
source_note: hedge: standard national antitrust doctrine distinguishing unilateral refusal to deal from concerted group boycotts, not Pennsylvania-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.305(a), under what business name may a brokerage company, including a sole proprietorship, cemetery company, or rental listing referral agency, advertise or hold itself out to the public?
choice_a: Only under the business name designated on its license
choice_b: Under any name the brokerage chooses at any given time, with no restriction
choice_c: Only under the name of its most senior salesperson
choice_d: Only under a name that has been separately trademarked with the USPTO
explanation: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.305(a) requires brokerage companies, sole proprietorships, cemetery companies, and rental listing referral agencies to advertise or otherwise hold themselves out to the public only under the business name designated on their license -- preventing entities from marketing under an unapproved alias.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.305(a) (confirmed, quoted via Cornell LII regulation excerpt)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.305(c), when an associate broker or salesperson advertises, what information about their employing broker must appear, and in what relative size?
choice_a: The employing broker's business name and telephone number must appear, and must be of EQUAL SIZE to the licensee's own name and telephone number in the advertisement
choice_b: No reference to the employing broker is required in a salesperson's individual advertisement
choice_c: The employing broker's information may appear in print so small it is illegible, so long as it is technically present
choice_d: Only the employing broker's name is required; a telephone number is never necessary
explanation: Section 35.305(c) requires that an advertisement by an associate broker, salesperson, cemetery associate broker, or cemetery salesperson contain the business name and telephone number of the employing broker, with those names and telephone numbers appearing in equal size to the licensee's own -- preventing a salesperson's ad from effectively obscuring who they work for.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.305(c) (confirmed, quoted via Cornell LII regulation excerpt)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.305(b), what must a licensee do before using and advertising a nickname in place of their legal first name?
choice_a: Include the nickname on their licensure application or biennial renewal application
choice_b: Nothing -- licensees may freely advertise under any nickname without ever notifying the Commission
choice_c: Obtain a court order legally changing their name
choice_d: File a separate fictitious-name registration exclusively for the nickname each year
explanation: Section 35.305(b) requires a licensee who wishes to use and advertise a nickname for their first name to include that nickname on their licensure or biennial renewal application -- ensuring the Commission's records tie the advertised nickname back to the licensee's actual licensed identity.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.305(b) (confirmed)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Licensing & Ethics
question: Under 49 Pa. Code Section 35.304, must a licensee who is personally selling or leasing their OWN real estate disclose their status as a real estate licensee in advertisements for that property?
choice_a: Yes, they must disclose that they are a real estate licensee in advertisements for the property -- UNLESS the property is listed with a real estate company
choice_b: No -- licensees selling their own property are never required to disclose their licensed status under any circumstance
choice_c: Yes, but only for commercial property; residential self-sales are exempt
choice_d: Disclosure is required only if the licensee is a broker, never for a salesperson
explanation: Section 35.304 requires a licensee selling or leasing their own real estate to disclose their status as a real estate licensee in the property's advertisements, since a buyer or tenant might otherwise assume they are dealing with an ordinary private seller/landlord rather than someone with professional real estate expertise -- but this requirement does not apply if the property is instead listed with a real estate company.
source_note: 49 Pa. Code Section 35.304 (confirmed, quoted via Cornell LII regulation excerpt; adopted February 1989, amended November 2000)
